transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-04
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (HelioRetail CTO), Samira Khan (HelioRetail Platform), Ethan Park (HelioRetail ML), Maya Torres (HelioRetail Security)

Summary:
Quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, parameter tuning, and retry/fallback patterns. Customer is evaluating for a product-recommendation chat widget with latency target ~200-400ms for short replies and cost sensitivity on token spend. They asked about VPC/dedicated options and audit artifacts.

Topics covered:
- Quick qualification: current stack, QPS, SLAs
- Live hosted API demo: streaming + chatgen params
- Retry and backoff patterns + graceful fallback to smaller model
- Console: routing and per-route cost breakdowns
- Optimize suggestions: batching/quantization recommendations
- Security: SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML notes

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. We'll do a short walk through of how our hosted ChatGen works with streaming and then dive into parameters and retries. Priya will run the demo.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, thanks. Quick context — HelioRetail runs a product chat widget on web and mobile. Typical query length is 8-40 tokens, average session 3-4 turns. Target latency for short answers is sub 400ms, cost is obviously important.
[00:35] Priya: Perfect, that helps. Do you have an estimate of QPS during peak?
[00:40] Samira: Peak is about 120 rps for the widget globally, but most regions are below 40 rps. We can burst but want predictable bills.
[00:52] Priya: Okay that maps well to hosted with autoscaling or Dedicated if you want capacity guarantees. For hosted we often advise route-level limits and batching tweaks; for Dedicated you get fixed GPU pools.
[01:08] Ethan: Quick sec — what does batching do for sub-100ms requests? Won't it add latency?
[01:15] Liam: Good call — batching is workload-aware. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching and will only batch when it helps throughput without pushing median latency past your SLO; also prefix/KV caching can avoid re-computation for repeated queries.
[01:33] Ethan: KV cash? (laughs)
[01:34] Priya: Yeah, KV cache — sometimes our transcriber writes it as "K-V cash" — it stores previous key-values so follow-ups skip full compute.
[01:45] Jordan: Can you show the streaming behavior? We need to see partial tokens arrive quickly and then completion.
[01:52] Priya: Sure — sharing my screen. Starting a simple chatgen call in the console sandbox. I'm using model: rwd-chat-medium (hosted baseline). Params: max_tokens 60, temperature 0.2, top_p 0.95, stream:true, stop sequences.
[02:15] Priya: Watch first response — you can see the initial chunk arrives quickly (about 120ms), subsequent tokens stream, and the final completion with finish_reason "stop". If a node hiccups, our client SDK handles SSE reconnects and we have idempotency tokens for safe retries.
[02:42] Samira: How do SDK reconnects work? Suppose a mobile client drops mid-stream — will we lose the partial?
[02:50] Priya: If the TCP breaks, the SDK can re-attach to the same response via the request id and idempotency-token; you'll either get the full response replayed or continue from cache if available. For mobile we recommend an optimistic UI that shows partials as they arrive and then reconciles on final completion.
[03:10] Jordan: And retries — what do you recommend for backoff strategy?
[03:15] Priya: Standard is exponential backoff with jitter, with a max retry count tuned by idempotency and request type. For generation we often do: 0s, 200ms, 600ms, 1800ms (three retries), but for low-latency customer flows you'd want aggressive early failover to a cost- and latency-optimized model.
[03:35] Ethan: So fallback to a smaller model for lower latency — is that automatic?
[03:39] Priya: We have route rules in the Console where you can set policy: if latency > X or error rate spike, route to a compatible smaller variant (e.g., rwd-chat-small-quant). That preserves UX while saving tokens.
[03:55] Maya: On security — we need SOC2, SAML SSO support and KMS for key management.
[04:01] Alex: We can provide SOC2 Type II report. For private key control, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM; for hosted we integrate with major cloud KMS options and support envelope encryption. SSO via SAML/Okta is available.
[04:20] Maya: Any gotchas on logs? We need to ensure sensitive PII isn't retained.
[04:25] Priya: You control retention at the route level. By default hosted API keeps logs for short window, but you can disable storing full payloads or enable always-on redaction. For Private you have full control.
[04:42] Jordan: Walk me through cost controls — how do you break down per-route token spend?
[04:49] Liam: Console shows token level breakdown by model and route. You can also pin default model per route and set soft limits. Optimize will suggest quantization or smaller model families for requests dominated by short replies.
[05:05] Ethan: Can Optimize propose quantization levels? We're testing 4-bit quant for some models.
[05:10] Priya: Yes Optimize will recommend quantization-friendly variants with a quality delta estimate based on your prompt set, and also propose batching or cache TTL settings to reduce per-token cost.
[05:25] Jordan: Can we see a prompt-level quality regression check? We want to ensure recommendations don't change UX.
[05:30] Priya: We have evals tied to prompt sets. You upload a set of representative prompts and Optimize runs an A/B to estimate quality drift and token savings, with example diffs surfaced in the Console.
[05:45] Samira: Cool. Could you show the retry logs when a generation fails?
[05:50] Priya: Switching to the trace view — here you can see a request timeline: initial attempt, error 503 at 0.3s, automatic retry with idempotency, then fallback to smaller model at 1.2s, and final success.
[06:12] Ethan: The timeline shows a big token spike on the fallback — is that because the smaller model produced longer output?
[06:18] Priya: Sometimes yes — fallback models may prefer different phrasing. We mitigate that with prompt templates and length controls. You can set max_output_tokens and arrival heuristics to keep responses short.
[06:33] Jordan: If we wanted dedicated, how long to provision and what's the SLA?
[06:39] Alex: Dedicated capacity is typically provisioned in 2-4 weeks depending on sizing and contract. We offer 99.9% uptime SLA and predictable throughput. For customers with 100+ rps sustained we often recommend a dedicated pool.
[06:54] Samira: Our big constraint is data residency — most EU traffic must keep logs in EU. Does hosted support region pinning?
[07:02] Liam: Hosted supports region routing and you can pin routes to EU regions; for strict residency you'd consider Private deployment in a customer VPC.
[07:12] Maya: On KMS integration — does the hosted option ever see unencrypted tokens in logs?
[07:18] Priya: No, payloads are encrypted at rest and in transit. We redact sensitive fields on ingest if you enable that policy; the retention controls are per-route.
[07:30] Jordan: Back to streaming — we noticed inconsistent partials in some demoed runs. Any causes?
[07:36] Priya: Partial stalls usually come from network jitter or node GC events. Our engineered guardrails prioritize sending initial tokens quickly; if a stall occurs the client SDK will surface progress and we can fall back to a short poll for the remainder.
[07:52] Ethan: For mobile, is there a recommended SDK?
[07:55] Priya: We have Node, Python, and lightweight JS SDKs; for native mobile we recommend a small relay (edge) or our mobile-optimized client that handles reconnects and idempotency.
[08:10] Jordan: Can you show the console route rule setup for a fallback?
[08:14] Priya: Yep — in Console -> Routing, you create a rule: if latency > 600ms for 30s then switch to rwd-chat-small-quant. You can also set percentage rollouts and canary checks.
[08:32] Samira: What about function calling / structured output? We need to extract product ids from answers sometimes.
[08:38] Priya: ChatGen supports structured output and tool calls. You can enforce JSON schema via function spec and set strict parsing flags; Console has a built-in parser test harness.
[08:52] Maya: Any compliance certs beyond SOC2?
[08:55] Alex: We have ISO27001 in progress and enterprise customers can get tailored attestation packages. We also support audit logs export to customer SIEMs.
[09:10] Jordan: Behaviorally, if we enable caching, does it create accidental stale responses when product catalog changes?
[09:17] Priya: Cache is TTL-based and keyed by prompt+context signature. For dynamic content like price, we advise bypassing cache for those requests or setting a short TTL and including a freshness token.
[09:34] Ethan: Could you run a small stress trace against a sample prompt? We want to see median p50 and p95.
[09:40] Priya: Sure — running a 1-minute synthetic at 50 rps with your sample prompts. (typing) Results: p50 ~ 180ms, p95 ~ 620ms on this model at current sandbox load. With prefix caching for repeated prompts p95 drops to ~320ms.
[10:05] Jordan: Those numbers look promising. How does token billing work for partial streaming?
[10:10] Liam: Billing is for tokens generated + input tokens. Partial streams still count generated tokens. For streaming interrupted by retries we charge only for final accepted tokens — retries that are idempotent don't double bill because we dedupe with request id on server side where possible.
[10:29] Samira: Any edge cases where double billing might occur?
[10:32] Priya: If you intentionally fire off duplicate requests without idempotency keys, you could be billed twice. Use idempotency for non-stateless calls.
[10:44] Ethan: For model selection — what's the tradeoff table?
[10:48] Liam: In Console we show performance profiles: latency vs cost vs quality. For example rwd-chat-large gives higher quality but 2-3x token cost and 40-60% more latency compared to rwd-chat-medium. Optimize suggests midpoints based on your prompt set.
[11:05] Jordan: Let's talk SLOs. Can Redwood emit traces to our APM?
[11:09] Priya: Yes, we integrate with Datadog, NewRelic, and support exporting trace spans. Console also exposes per-request traces.
[11:20] Samira: Any plan for per-token throttling?
[11:24] Alex: We support per-route quotas and rate limits. You can throttle either by rps or estimated token spend.
[11:32] Jordan: Good. On the pilot — can we run a 2-week hosted pilot with a constraint that we can cap monthly spend?
[11:38] Alex: Yes, we can set spend caps for the pilot and export usage reports daily. We'll include that in the pricing doc.
[11:45] Maya: Security wants to review the ingestion pipeline diagram.
[11:49] Alex: We'll attach the architecture and SOC2 artefacts in the follow up.
[11:55] Ethan: A couple of questions from engineering: how to control hallucinations & answer safety?
[12:00] Priya: We recommend prompt engineering + system message templates, temperature tuning (lower for factual outputs), and post-filtering via safety checks. Optimize can suggest temperature/top_p combos and warn on regression.
[12:18] Jordan: Show me the SDK snippet to set idempotency and stream handling.
[12:22] Priya: (reads snippet) const resp = await client.chat.create({ model: 'rwd-chat-medium', messages, stream: true, idempotency_key: 'abc-123', max_tokens: 80 }); resp.on('data', chunk => { /* append partial */ });
[12:40] Samira: That idempotency_key — is it a TTL-ed server-side dedupe?
[12:44] Priya: Yes, server maintains dedupe window (configurable). If it sees same idempotency key within window, it dedupes.
[12:52] Ethan: If our client uses a CDN edge relay that batches many users, any recommended pattern?
[12:57] Liam: Use an edge pool with per-user correlation and don't collapse idempotency across users. We also recommend adding a small jitter to avoid thundering herd.
[13:10] Jordan: Can we configure regional failover? If EU region has an outage, route to US for non-sensitive traffic?
[13:16] Priya: Yes. We have routing policies by region and sensitivity tag. You can set fallback to a different region only for non-PII routes.
[13:30] Samira: One more on console — is there a bulk edit for route rules and environment variables?
[13:34] Liam: Yes, Console supports CSV import and API for infra as code to manage routes.
[13:43] Jordan: Anything else we should watch out for in onboarding?
[13:46] Alex: Make sure you have a representative prompt set, define acceptance criteria for quality and latency, and pick a pilot scope (e.g., web widget only). Priya will run the baseline.
[13:58] Priya: Running through a small failure simulation: I'll simulate an injected 503 on the primary route. You can see retry attempts and then automatic failover to the fallback model, and the SDK logs show reconnection attempts.
[14:18] Ethan: The console shows a spike in errors at t=0.4s but final success at t=1.6s. Looks acceptable for non-blocking flows.
[14:27] Jordan: For the production rollout, can we do percentage-based gradual rollouts?
[14:31] Priya: Absolutely — Console supports canary rollouts with automatic rollback on error rate or regression signals from evals.
[14:42] Maya: A quick question on retention — can we keep logs for 30 days only and then purge?
[14:47] Priya: Yes, retention is configurable by route.
[14:50] Alex: Okay quick recap & next steps?
[14:54] Jordan: Sounds good.
[15:00] Recap (Alex): We'll send pricing and pilot checklist; SEs will run baseline test and share latency traces; security will exchange SOC2 & KMS notes. Customer to confirm pilot window availability. Any final questions?
[15:20] Samira: No, that covers it.
[15:22] Ethan: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript fidelity: speaker labels sometimes generic, occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., "KV cash"), and timestamps are approximate.
